blocks.text: Hello Michelle,

That is a welcome way to close the question, and our thanks go to whoever on your team ran the new extract so quickly. I have marked the duplicated records as closed in our request log, with a note that the original file was replaced rather than adjusted, so there is a clear trail if anyone later asks how the reserve detail for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} came to agree with the year-end figures.

As David says, the checks on the individual fields come next, and he expects to start on them tomorrow. If they turn up anything that needs your team's knowledge of the records, it will reach you from me, the same way as before, along with a note of what we would assume in the meantime, so that you are never left wondering what we have done with a record.

That leaves one item open from our original request: the documentation of the methods and assumptions behind the current reserves, including any change made during the year. Jennifer can begin her part of the review as soon as it arrives, so it is the thing we would most like to have from you next.
Best,
Reserve Adequacy Review for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}

A briefing for Michelle Hudson, Director of Operations, prepared by Megan Dudley with Jennifer Vasquez and David Sherman. It covers where the work stands, what the data have shown us so far, and what we will be asking of your team over the coming weeks.
Where the work stands

We have been at work since {{fact:f:E-2017-001.start}}, and nearly all of that time has gone into the data, as the engagement letter said it would. Using the replacement extract your team ran for us, the reserve detail now agrees with your year-end figures within rounding, and our data log records why the first file was set aside.
What the records are telling us

David Sherman has moved on from totals to the individual fields the model draws on, and most records are clean. A small group carries an incurred date later than the valuation date, which cannot be right for a reserve held at that date. Until we hear otherwise we are using each claim's reported date in its place, and we have written that down as our assumption, not as something the file told us.
Your methods and assumptions

The documentation of the methods and assumptions behind the current reserves has arrived, and Jennifer Vasquez is working through it. She is sorting the assumptions into those that are prescribed and those that rest on judgment, and looking closely at the one change it records during the year. We have formed no view on any of them yet, and nothing in this briefing should be read as a finding.
Who is doing what

Jennifer Vasquez leads the review and remains your first call on scope, schedule, and questions of judgment. David Sherman builds the reserve model and carries the reconciliation. Megan Dudley keeps the request log and stays your contact for anything to do with files, so that your staff hear about data from one person on our side.
From here

Once the incurred dates are settled, David Sherman will reproduce your carried reserves with your own methods, which is the step before we build an estimate of our own. We would like to hold a working session with you in November to go through the data position and the assumption questions together. The one thing we need before then is a word from your team on how those incurred dates came to be entered.
Reserve Adequacy Review: Working Session Minutes

Summary: the data position for the review is settled. Two questions bearing on the assumptions remain open, and both must be resolved before work can begin on an independent estimate of the reserves {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} requires. Each open item has an owner in the table at the end of these minutes.
Attendees
Discussion

1. Data. David Sherman reported that the field-level checks on the replacement extract are complete. Apart from the records with an incurred date later than the valuation date, raised in October, the fields the model draws on are internally consistent. Michelle Hudson confirmed that those dates were keyed in error. Corrected dates have been supplied and loaded, and the reported date is no longer being used in their place. The data log shows the original entry, the correction, and its source.

2. Replication. David Sherman has reproduced the carried reserves using the client's own methods and assumptions. The reproduction agrees with the carried total closely enough to show that the model reads the records the way the client's process does. A small residual difference has not yet been traced and is not being treated as a finding. No estimate of our own has been produced, and none was presented at the session.

3. Methods and assumptions. Jennifer Vasquez summarized her review of the documentation. The assumptions divide into those that are prescribed and those that rest on judgment, and the second group is where the review will concentrate. The documentation records one change of assumption during the year but does not include the analysis that supported it. Michelle Hudson undertook to locate that analysis.

4. Experience period. Michelle Hudson reported that the claim system was replaced partway through the period covered by the claim history, and that claim handling practice changed at about the same time. Jennifer Vasquez noted that if the earlier experience reflects a different practice, it may not be a reliable guide to how the current claims will run off. The choice of period is a matter of actuarial judgment and will be documented as such in the report. She asked for a written description of what changed and when, so that the choice rests on the client's account rather than on an inference from the data. No decision on the period was taken.

5. Requests and timetable. Megan Dudley confirmed that every item on the original data request has now been received. The work is on the schedule set out in the engagement letter. The next working session will review preliminary estimates, once the first two action items below are complete and the period has been settled.
Action items

rows: Provide a written description of the claim system replacement and the change in claim handling practice, including when each took effect.
Locate the analysis that supported the assumption change made during the year.
Send the client a short note setting out the candidate experience periods and how each would be tested.
Trace the residual difference in the replication and record the explanation in the data log.
Log items 1 and 2 on receipt and circulate them to the team.

blocks.text: Reserve Adequacy Review: Progress Report

Prepared for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} by Megan Dudley, with Jennifer Vasquez and David Sherman. This report covers our work since the October briefing, including the working session in November, and looks ahead to the part of the review that produces our own estimate.
Where the review stands

We are roughly halfway through the review, and the part we expected to take longest is now behind us. The data are settled. The reserve detail reconciles to your year-end figures, the individual fields our model relies on have been checked, and every item on our original request has been received. David Sherman has also reproduced your carried reserves using your own methods and assumptions, which tells us that the model reads the records the same way your process does. What we have not yet done, and have deliberately held back from, is form any view of our own on whether the reserves are adequate. That is the work of the next phase.
The time charged so far sits within the budget of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.fee}} set out in our engagement letter, and on what we know today we expect the remaining work to fit within it as well.
What we completed this period

Most of these weeks went to the data, as we said they would. Once the replacement extract had resolved the duplicated records, David Sherman moved from totals to the fields themselves. That work found one real problem, a small group of records whose incurred date fell after the valuation date. For a time we used the date each claim was reported in its place, and noted that in our working papers, so that the reconciliation could keep moving. Your team then confirmed that the dates had been keyed in error and sent corrected ones, which are now loaded. Our provisional treatment has been withdrawn, and the data log shows the original entry, the correction, and where the correction came from.

Alongside that, Jennifer Vasquez has worked through the documentation of your methods and assumptions. She has sorted the assumptions into those that are prescribed and those that rest on judgment, and it is the second group where our attention will go from here. The documentation records one change of assumption made during the year, and the analysis behind that change has since reached us. We are grateful to your team for finding it, since it lets us review the change on the basis your team actually used.

The November session was, for us, the most useful conversation of the engagement so far. Learning that the claim system was replaced partway through the period our claim history covers, and that claim handling changed around the same time, has shaped our thinking about the assumptions more than anything in the files could have.
The work ahead

Our main task now is to build our own estimate of the reserves required. Before we can build it, one judgment has to be made, and it is ours to make: whether the claim experience from before the system replacement belongs in the period we use to set our assumptions. If claims were handled differently then, the older experience may describe a pattern that no longer applies, and relying on it could make the reserves look stronger or weaker than they are. Jennifer Vasquez set out the candidate periods in her note after the session. We intend to build the estimate on one period and show the other alongside it, so that anyone reading the report can see how much the choice matters.

Once the estimate is built, David Sherman will compare it with the carried reserves and trace any difference to its source, whether that is the data, the method, or an assumption. Jennifer Vasquez will review each exhibit before it leaves our office. We expect to bring preliminary results to a working session early in the new year and to follow that with the draft report, which will keep what the data show, what we assumed, and what we conclude in separate places, as the engagement letter promised.
What could move the timetable

The item we are watching most closely is the written description of the system replacement and the change in claim handling, which we asked for at the session and which has not yet arrived. We would much prefer to base the choice of period on your own account of what changed, because an inference drawn from the data alone is harder to defend in a report that will be read by people who were not in the room. If the description has not reached us by the time the estimate is ready to run, we will go ahead on our reading of the data, test both periods, and say plainly in the report that the choice rests on our inference, not on your records.

The holiday weeks are the other thing on our minds, simply because a question that would normally be answered in a day can take a week at this time of year, so we have tried to ask for everything we can foresee needing before then. The small residual difference in the replication has not yet been fully explained. We mention it only so that it does not come as a surprise later; it is not a finding, and David Sherman expects to account for it before the estimate is run.
What we need from you

The one thing we need next is that written description of the claim system replacement and the change in claim handling that came with it, including when each took effect. I will log it as soon as it arrives and pass it to Jennifer Vasquez the same day.
Minutes: Session on the Draft Report

The session took {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}'s questions on the draft report. Three revisions to the draft were agreed, together with a one-page summary to accompany the final report. None of them alters our estimate or its comparison with the carried reserves, and the final report can be prepared once they are made.
Present
Questions raised on the draft

Data section. Michelle Hudson asked that the account of the replaced extract state plainly that the replacement was a fresh run of the same extract as of the same valuation date, not a corrected copy of the first file. David Sherman agreed that the current wording could be read either way. The paragraph on the misdated records will also say that the corrected dates were supplied by the client and loaded as received, not estimated by us.

Experience period. The draft sets the assumptions on claim experience after the claim system replacement and shows the effect of including the earlier experience as a sensitivity. Michelle Hudson asked whether the sensitivity should be read as a second estimate. Jennifer Vasquez said it should not. The choice of period is a judgment, documented in the assumptions section with the client's written description of the change as its basis. The sensitivity is shown so that a reader can see how much that judgment matters. The paragraph introducing the exhibit will be revised to say so.
Assumption change made during the year. The analysis that supported the change is cited in the draft by description only. Michelle Hudson asked that the citation name the document. Agreed.

Summary for management. Michelle Hudson asked whether a one-page summary could be prepared for her management. Jennifer Vasquez agreed, on the condition that the summary carries the conclusion together with the assumptions it depends on and refers the reader to the full report. A summary that states the conclusion without its assumptions will not be issued.

Replication residual. Michelle Hudson asked whether the small difference in the replication, mentioned in the December progress report, had been explained. David Sherman said it had. It comes from the client's process rounding its reserve factors before applying them, where the model carries them unrounded. The effect is described in the data section and is immaterial to the comparison. It is not a finding about the reserves.

Timing. Jennifer Vasquez confirmed that the final report will follow once the revisions below are made and item 5 has been answered. No change to the schedule in the engagement letter is expected. Any questions that follow from this session will be handled as part of the one round of questions on the draft that the letter provides for.
Agreed actions

items: 1. Revise the data section's account of the replaced extract and the corrected dates. Owner: Megan Dudley, with David Sherman checking the wording against the data log.
2. Revise the paragraph introducing the sensitivity exhibit. Owner: Jennifer Vasquez.
3. Name the supporting analysis in the assumptions section, using its title as logged on receipt. Owner: Megan Dudley.
4. Draft the one-page summary, to be issued with the final report. Owner: Jennifer Vasquez.
5. Confirm whether any further questions on the draft will come from {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}. Owner: Michelle Hudson.

blocks.text: Any further questions on the draft should come to Megan Dudley, as the data questions did, so that one log holds them all.
